planting.note: Plant in spring after all frost danger has passed in very well-drained, gritty, low-fertility soil in full sun; Impala Lily is grown in containers outside zone 10-12 and brought indoors or to a frost-free location well before cold weather, since it cannot tolerate temperatures below about 40F.

directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, gritty, low-fertility soil, letting the soil dry between waterings; Impala Lily is a southern African relative of the more commonly grown Adenium obesum, distinguished by its distinctive winter-into-early-spring bloom timing (opposite the summer-blooming obesum) and its showy flowers, which are white to pale pink at the base and flare into a deep crimson-red margin, resembling the leaping impala antelope that gives the plant its common name in its native range. Unlike Adenium obesum, this species typically drops its leaves and flowers before or during bloom, producing a striking floral display on bare stems reminiscent of a flowering fruit tree. It develops the same swollen, water-storing caudex at the base of the stem as its relative, becoming more sculptural and valuable with age, and shares the same need for a frost-free winter location and reduced watering during its natural dry-season dormancy. All parts of the plant contain toxic cardiac glycosides and should be kept away from children and pets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in full sun in sandy, extremely well-drained soil; Pachypodium geayi is frost-sensitive and cannot tolerate temperatures below about 40F, so grow as a large container specimen moved indoors for winter outside of zone 10-12. The plant drops its leaves in winter dormancy; resume watering when new growth appears in spring.

directions: Plant in full sun in sandy, gravelly, or any extremely well-draining soil medium, since this Madagascar succulent tree rots quickly in heavy or moisture-retentive soil. Pachypodium geayi is very similar to and frequently confused with the more common Pachypodium lamerei in the nursery trade, but can be distinguished by its narrower, longer, more silvery-gray leaves with fine hairs along the margins, giving the crown a softer, more silvered appearance than lamerei's broader, glossier green leaves. Like its relative, it grows as a tall, spine-covered succulent column that is not a true palm despite the common name, eventually branching with age and producing fragrant, pinwheel-shaped white flowers at the stem tips on mature specimens grown in strong light. The milky sap is toxic and irritating to skin and eyes, so wear gloves when pruning or repotting, and site the sharp, spine-covered trunk away from foot traffic.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, well-drained, humus-amended soil in shade to partial shade; Metallic Palm has little cold tolerance and is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11, elsewhere as a shade-loving houseplant.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade to bright indirect light; Metallic Palm is a compact, slow-growing understory palm from the rainforests of southern Mexico, valued for its unusual undivided, broad, blue-green leaflets with an iridescent, metallic-blue sheen that catches the light quite differently from the finely divided fronds of most other parlor-type Chamaedorea palms. It stays small and clumping, rarely exceeding 5-6 feet, making it well suited to shaded patios, atriums, and as a long-lived houseplant that tolerates the low light of typical indoor rooms better than nearly any other palm. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and mist occasionally or provide a humidity tray, since dry indoor air can cause brown leaf tips. It is dioecious, so both a male and female plant are needed for the small orange fruit to form, though most home growers keep it purely for its striking foliage.
